# What do PISA test results have to do with families, work, and the future?

**The PISA tests are not just a diagnostic tool for school performance. Their results allow us to identify the level of competence in reading, mathematics, and science that underpins later learning, the ability to solve problems, and the development of skills necessary for academic and professional life.**

**In Colombia, recent results reveal challenges that require attention beyond the classroom, with a collective and sustained commitment. Families, schools, universities, the public sector, and businesses all have different responsibilities regarding the strengthening of these skills.**

- What do PISA test results have to do with families, work, and the future?

![Image: What do PISA test results have to do with families, work, and the future?](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/59cd5b4a-416c-406a-9748-a9141d306d23/web/resultados-pruebas-pisa-familias-trabajo-futuro-nota-graduados.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=yn6nYTjl)

The PISA results pose challenges that transcend the classroom and require the participation of different actors in society.

Reading a news article, understanding task instructions, interpreting a number, or deciding whether information is reliable seem like everyday actions. Behind each of these are skills that begin to develop in early childhood and remain necessary long after school ends. Therefore, when the PISA tests ( [Programme for International Student Assessment](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/pisa.html) , created and organized by the OECD) reveal difficulties in competencies such as reading comprehension and mathematics, the question should not only be how to improve results in the next assessment, but also what each stakeholder can do to strengthen the learning that these results highlight.

For Claudia Restrepo Montoya, president of EAFIT University, the results should lead to a deeper analysis. “Exposure to screens has accelerated people's difficulty concentrating, and this generates a decrease in literacy skills. Clearly, the habits developed at home are important, but we have been losing skills for years. We have to change models in primary and secondary education and at the university level as well, because we need to level the playing field,” she states.

César Tamayo Tobón, dean of the School of Finance, Economics, and Government at EAFIT, agrees, noting that the results also pose challenges for higher education institutions that receive students with diverse educational backgrounds. “PISA captures learning and is a predictor of future performance in technical skills, at university, and also in terms of productivity. Universities cannot change what happened when students were 15 years old, but we can make an additional effort to close those gaps when they reach higher education,” he explains.

However, addressing these difficulties also requires examining the earlier stages of education. For Lorena María Quiroz Betancur, a professor in the Faculty of Education at the University of Antioquia, the PISA results demonstrate the need to strengthen the connection between educational institutions, teachers, and families, especially in a context marked by the increasing use of technology.

“Given this scenario, the call goes beyond simply focusing efforts on achieving high scores. The real challenge lies in finding points of convergence that allow us to integrate the use of emerging technologies, family support, and the recognition and attention to diversity, with the aim of fostering experiential, inclusive, and transformative educational environments,” the professor explains.

##### Read to learn

While PISA results cover competencies such as reading, mathematics, and science, reading comprehension plays a cross-cutting role: it allows individuals to interpret instructions, access information, understand other content, and make decisions based on what they read. Therefore, strengthening reading comprehension is not just about improving a specific skill, but about creating conditions for lifelong learning.

Sandra Zuluaga, director of the Ratón de Biblioteca Foundation, explains that learning to read is a process that begins in school, but requires prerequisites and constant support. “Before formally learning to read and write, children need to talk, listen to stories, sing, play with words, and have contact with books. And when they start school, especially in first grade, learning to read becomes a gateway to other learning. If this process is delayed, it can also affect the child's relationship with school and their interest in learning.”

This perspective also places families and caregivers in an important position. It's not about shifting the responsibility for outcomes onto them, but rather recognizing that many habits that foster learning are built in everyday life. Reading together, discussing what is read, asking why something happens, listening to children and young people, and introducing them to different types of texts are all actions that can complement the work of educational institutions.

Para Santiago Silva Jaramillo, ex secretario de Cultura Ciudadana de Medellín y profesor de la escuela de Artes y Humanidades de EAFIT, esa tarea convoca a buena parte de la sociedad. “La promoción de la lectura como hábito nos involucra a todos los ciudadanos. Involucra a instituciones que van desde los gobiernos locales y nacionales, que establecen políticas de promoción de lectura, a las universidades, que reciben y que pueden adoptar y seguir promoviendo hábitos lectores, a los papás y a los cuidadores, que también los pueden promover en sus hogares, y evidentemente a las instituciones educativas”, afirma.

De igual forma, la conversación también toca las puertas del sector productivo. Las empresas reciben a personas que han recorrido distintas etapas del sistema educativo y requieren habilidades esenciales. Como señala la rectora Claudia Restrepo, su papel no consiste en sustituir las funciones de colegios o universidades, sino en reconocer que la formación del talento es un proceso de largo plazo y que pueden contribuir mediante alianzas, experiencias de formación y oportunidades para que los jóvenes desarrollen esas capacidades.

Así, PISA puede entenderse menos como una fotografía que aparece cada cierto tiempo y más como una señal para revisar lo que ocurre de manera cotidiana en el sistema educativo y en la sociedad. Colegios, universidades, familias, bibliotecas, empresas, gobiernos y ciudadanos tienen roles distintos en el desarrollo de las competencias que permiten aprender a lo largo de la vida. La discusión, entonces, no termina cuando se conocen los resultados de una prueba: empieza cuando cada actor reconoce qué puede hacer a partir de lo que estos resultados están mostrando y convierte esa señal en decisiones y acciones sostenidas.
